Memo from People Operations, Halvorsen Instruments, 18 December 2026. Subject: year-end leave carryover query for Tomas Bekele.

Tomas Bekele has asked whether he may carry seven days of unused annual leave from 2026 into 2027. His manager supports the request but wants confirmation that it is permitted under the Leave Policy before approving it in the system.

The relevant policy is the Annual Leave Policy, revision 5, which reads in part as follows.

Under the standard carryover rule (paragraph 6.1), an employee may carry no more than five days of unused annual leave into the following calendar year. Any balance above the carryover limit is forfeited on 31 December unless the employee has a written agreement approved by the Chief People Officer before 1 December.

Paragraph 6.2 provides an exception for employees who were on parental leave for any part of the fourth quarter: such employees may carry their full unused balance into the following year without limit. Tomas was not on parental leave at any point in 2026.

Paragraph 6.4 deals with a different leave type and is included here for completeness: sick leave does not accrue and does not carry over under any circumstances, and unused sick days have no cash value on termination.

Paragraph 2 contains the definitions. "Continuous service" is measured from the employee's original start date with the company, and includes any period worked under a fixed-term or temporary contract with the company that was followed without a break of more than 30 days by a permanent appointment. Periods worked through an external agency are excluded.

Amendment 3 to the policy, issued 4 November 2026 and stated to apply to the 2026-to-2027 transition and thereafter, raises the carryover limit in paragraph 6.1 from five days to eight days for employees with at least five years of continuous service as at 31 December of the year in which the leave was earned. The five-day limit continues to apply to all other employees. The amendment states that where it conflicts with paragraph 6.1, the amendment governs.

Tomas's employment history, taken from the HR system: he began on 15 March 2021 on a twelve-month fixed-term contract directly with Halvorsen Instruments as a calibration technician; the contract ended 14 March 2022; he was appointed to a permanent position on 21 March 2022 and has been employed continuously since. He has no written carryover agreement on file.

question.instructions: Does the Annual Leave Policy permit Tomas Bekele to carry seven days of unused leave into 2027?

criteria.true: The carryover of seven days is within the limit that applies to him.
criteria.false: The carryover of seven days exceeds the limit that applies to him, or is otherwise not permitted.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-train-mixed
provenance.rationale: Amendment 3 raises the limit to eight days for employees with five years of continuous service at 31 December 2026. Under paragraph 2, continuous service runs from the original start date and includes his fixed-term contract because the gap before the permanent appointment was seven days, under 30. Service therefore began 15 March 2021, which is more than five years by 31 December 2026. Seven days is within the eight-day limit; the parental leave exception is irrelevant.
provenance.why_hard: Counting service from the permanent appointment in March 2022 gives under five years and leaves the five-day limit in place, which is the obvious but wrong reading.

IT Service Desk internal note, ticket HD-51877, prepared by the hardware coordinator for the desk lead.

Priya Anand, an account manager in the Commercial team, has asked for her laptop to be replaced. The device is a Corvex 14 issued on 20 January 2024, which makes it 32 months old at the time of the request. The hinge has failed and the screen no longer stays open. The authorised repairer has quoted 410 for the hinge and bezel repair. The current replacement value of a Corvex 14 on our standard catalogue is 1,050.

The Endpoint Hardware Standard, edition 3, governs replacement. Its base rule (section 4.1) is that a laptop becomes eligible for scheduled replacement once it has been in service for 36 months, measured from the issue date recorded in the asset register. Before 36 months the device is repaired rather than replaced.

Section 4.2 sets out an early-replacement exception: a device may be replaced before its scheduled date where the quoted cost of repair exceeds 50 percent of the current replacement value, or where the device has had two or more hardware repairs already recorded against it. The asset register shows no prior repairs for this device.

Section 4.5 concerns peripherals and is a separate matter: monitors, docks, keyboards and headsets are replaced on request when faulty, without reference to age, and are not subject to the 36-month cycle.

Section 2 gives definitions. A "field role" is a role listed in Appendix A of the Standard; the list is maintained by People Operations and is the only source used to determine field status. The appendix currently lists field service engineers, sales engineers and site auditors. Account managers are not listed, although the coordinator notes that several of them travel frequently.

Amendment 2 to the Standard, effective 1 July 2026, shortens the replacement cycle in section 4.1 from 36 months to 30 months for devices assigned to employees in field roles. It states that it does not alter section 4.2 and that, where it conflicts with the base text, the amendment applies.

The coordinator's question is whether the device qualifies for replacement now rather than repair.

question.instructions: Under the Endpoint Hardware Standard as amended, is Priya Anand's laptop eligible for replacement now?

criteria.true: The device meets a replacement condition under the Standard as amended.
criteria.false: The device meets no replacement condition and must be repaired.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-train-mixed
provenance.rationale: The 30-month cycle in Amendment 2 applies only to field roles, which Appendix A defines exhaustively; account managers are not listed, so the 36-month cycle applies and 32 months is short of it. The early-replacement exception needs a repair quote above 50 percent of replacement value; 410 is about 39 percent of 1,050, and there are no prior repairs. Neither route qualifies.
provenance.why_hard: The 30-month amendment and the frequent-travel remark make the device look eligible, but field status is determined only by the appendix list.

Customer Care escalation summary, Okonkwo Outdoor Supply, prepared 14 September 2026.

A customer, order 5590231, wrote in asking for a price adjustment. He bought a two-person tent on 1 September for 189.00. On 10 September the same tent was sold at 129.00 during the "Ten-Hour Trail Sale", which ran from 08:00 to 18:00 that day and then reverted to 189.00. He is asking for the 60.00 difference. His account shows he is not enrolled in the Summit membership programme; he has a standard account created in 2024.

The agent handling the ticket has referred it because the Price Protection Policy was amended recently and the agent is not certain how the amendment interacts with the older text.

Price Protection Policy, section A, the base rule: if the price of an item purchased on the store falls within 14 days of the purchase date, the customer may request a one-time adjustment equal to the difference, refunded to the original payment method.

Section B, exclusions: no adjustment is given where the lower price was offered only during a flash sale. Section B also excludes clearance markdowns and open-box listings.

Section C, competitor price matching, is a separate programme: the store will match a lower price at an approved list of competing retailers if the customer provides a link within 7 days of purchase. Section C does not apply to the store's own price changes and has its own approval desk.

Section D, definitions: "purchase date" means the date the order was placed, not the delivery date. "Flash sale" means any promotional price that is in effect for fewer than 24 consecutive hours. "Summit member" means a customer enrolled in the Summit membership programme at the time of the adjustment request. Where an amendment conflicts with sections A to C, the amendment controls for requests made after its effective date.

Amendment 4, effective 15 September 2026: the flash-sale exclusion in section B no longer applies to Summit members. For Summit members a flash-sale price counts as a qualifying price drop under section A. The amendment makes no other change and states that section B continues to apply in full to all other customers.

The request was received on 12 September 2026. The 14-day window from the purchase date would run to 15 September.

question.instructions: Is the customer entitled to the 60.00 price adjustment under the Price Protection Policy?

criteria.true: The adjustment is available under the governing sections.
criteria.false: The adjustment is excluded or otherwise unavailable.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-train-mixed
provenance.rationale: The price drop occurred within 14 days of the purchase date, so section A is engaged. But the lower price was in effect for ten hours, which is a flash sale under section D, and section B excludes flash sales. Amendment 4 lifts that exclusion only for Summit members and only for requests after 15 September; this customer is not a member and requested on 12 September. Section C is about competitors and does not help.
provenance.why_hard: The timing fits section A and the amendment reads like it removes the flash-sale exclusion, but it is limited to members and to requests after its effective date.

Account review memo, Vesterlund Cloud Services, Customer Success, 6 October 2026. Subject: September SLA credit request from Farrow Logistics (Business tier).

Farrow Logistics has asked for a service credit for September 2026. Their account is on the Business tier. During September the platform recorded two outages affecting their region: an unplanned incident on 9 September lasting 20 minutes, and a maintenance window on 21 September during which the service was unavailable for 90 minutes. The maintenance was posted on the public status page on 17 September at 10:00, and the window began on 21 September at 10:00, so notice was given four days ahead. September has 30 days, which is 43,200 minutes.

The Service Level Agreement, version 3, provides as follows.

Clause 2, the uptime commitment: for the Business tier, monthly availability is committed at 99.9 percent. Where availability in a calendar month falls below the commitment, the customer is entitled to a credit of 10 percent of that month's fee on request. Clause 2 also states that the Enterprise tier commitment is 99.95 percent with a 25 percent credit; that tier is not relevant to Farrow, which has never been on it.

Clause 3, exclusions: downtime during scheduled maintenance is excluded from the availability calculation provided the maintenance was announced at least 72 hours in advance. Downtime caused by the customer's own network or by a third-party provider named in the customer's order form is also excluded.

Clause 5, definitions: "announced" means a post on the public status page; emails to account contacts do not count as an announcement for the purposes of clause 3. "Availability" is the percentage of minutes in the calendar month during which the service was reachable, after excluded minutes are removed from both numerator and denominator.

Clause 7, precedence: where an amendment published after this version conflicts with any clause, the amendment governs from its effective date for all customers on the affected tier.

Amendment SLA-3A, effective 1 September 2026, applies to the Business tier only. It changes the advance-notice requirement in clause 3 from 72 hours to 5 days (120 hours). The stated reason is that Business customers requested longer planning lead time. No other clause is changed.

The account manager's initial view, before reading the amendment, was that the 90 minutes of maintenance were excluded and that the 20 unplanned minutes alone would leave availability above 99.9 percent.

question.instructions: Is Farrow Logistics entitled to the September service credit under the SLA as amended?

criteria.true: September availability falls below the commitment that applies, so the credit is due.
criteria.false: September availability meets the commitment that applies, so no credit is due.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-train-mixed
provenance.rationale: Amendment SLA-3A requires 120 hours of status-page notice for Business tier maintenance to be excluded; the 21 September window was announced 96 hours ahead, so its 90 minutes count as downtime. Total downtime is 110 minutes out of 43,200, giving availability of about 99.75 percent, below the 99.9 percent commitment. The credit is due.
provenance.why_hard: Under the original 72-hour rule the maintenance would be excluded and only 20 minutes would count, which comfortably meets 99.9 percent; the amended notice period is the only thing that changes the outcome.

Shift note from the receiving supervisor, Kestrel Distribution Centre, 22 September 2026, for the compliance lead.

A pallet arrived this morning from a new supplier containing 40 cartons of "Solvent Wipes Pro", a cleaning product. The safety data sheet classifies the contents as Class 3 flammable liquid. Each carton is a single sealed package with a net contents of 3 kg. The receiving clerk put the pallet on hold in the dock area and asked whether it can go to Zone C, which is our general ambient storage, because Zone H, the hazardous store, is nearly full this week.

The Hazardous Goods Storage Procedure, issue 6, sets the rule. Under paragraph 3.1, goods classified as dangerous under Classes 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 must be stored only in Zone H, which has the fire suppression and bunding required for them.

Paragraph 3.3 provides a limited-quantity exception: packages of dangerous goods where each individual package contains no more than 5 kg (or 5 litres) may be stored in general ambient zones, provided they are palletised, labelled and kept at least 3 metres from any exit. The exception exists for consumer-sized retail packs that would not sensibly be routed to the hazardous store.

Paragraph 3.5 deals with perishable and temperature-controlled goods, which are unrelated to this question: chilled and frozen goods go to Zone K regardless of any other classification, and the limited-quantity exception has no bearing on them.

Paragraph 2 defines terms. "Package" means the smallest sealed unit as received, so a carton received sealed is one package even if it contains smaller retail units inside. "Class" refers to the class stated on the supplier's safety data sheet. Paragraph 2 also says that where a later amendment sets a different threshold from paragraph 3.3, the amendment's threshold applies to the classes it names and paragraph 3.3 continues to apply to all other classes.

Amendment 6-2, issued 1 August 2026 following a fire risk assessment, reduces the limited-quantity threshold in paragraph 3.3 to 1 kg (or 1 litre) per package for Class 3 flammable liquids only. Other classes remain at 5 kg. The amendment applies to all goods received on or after its issue date.

The compliance lead is asked whether the pallet may be placed in Zone C.

question.instructions: Under the procedure as amended, may the Solvent Wipes Pro pallet be stored in Zone C?

criteria.true: The pallet falls within an exception that allows general ambient storage.
criteria.false: The pallet must go to Zone H and may not be stored in Zone C.

provenance.author: claude-drafter-train-mixed
provenance.rationale: The contents are Class 3, so paragraph 3.1 requires Zone H unless the limited-quantity exception applies. Amendment 6-2 lowers that exception's threshold to 1 kg per package for Class 3 only. Release management note, Corvina mobile app team, 16 September 2026, for the release captain.

Bug MOB-4180 has been proposed for inclusion in the hotfix train that ships tomorrow. The bug is that the in-app document scanner crops the top 15 percent of a page when the device is in landscape orientation. It was found by QA during the 4.3 regression pass. QA has verified that the same steps on build 4.2.6, the previous release, produce a correctly cropped image, and that on 4.3.0, the current production build, the crop is wrong. Triage has assigned the bug priority P2. No customer has raised it, and there is no committed fix date on any customer account.

The Hotfix Admission Policy, revision 2, governs what may ship in a hotfix. The base rule, in section 1, is that only defects with priority P1 are admitted to a hotfix train; everything else waits for the next scheduled release.

Section 2 provides an exception: a P2 defect may be admitted where a customer has been given a committed fix date in writing by the account team and that date falls before the next scheduled release. The exception requires the account team to attach the commitment to the ticket.

Section 3 concerns feature requests and small enhancements, which are a different category: they are never admitted to a hotfix train, even where a customer has a commitment, and are handled through the roadmap process instead.

Section 4 gives definitions. "Regression" means a defect where the affected behaviour worked correctly in the immediately preceding production release and QA has recorded the comparison in the ticket. A defect that has existed across several releases is not a regression even if it was only recently noticed. "Current release" means the build presently in production.

Section 5 says that later amendments prevail over sections 1 to 3 where they conflict.

Amendment R2-1, effective 1 September 2026, adds a second exception: a P2 defect is admitted to a hotfix train if it is a regression, as defined in section 4, introduced in the current release. The amendment does not require a customer commitment for this route and states that section 2 continues to apply unchanged for non-regression P2 defects.

The release captain wants to know whether MOB-4180 can be admitted to tomorrow's hotfix.

question.instructions: Under the Hotfix Admission Policy as amended, may MOB-4180 be admitted to the hotfix train?

criteria.true: The defect satisfies an admission route under the policy.
criteria.false: The defect satisfies no admission route under the policy.

provenance.rationale: MOB-4180 is P2, so section 1 alone would exclude it, and there is no customer commitment for section 2. Amendment R2-1 admits such P2 regressions without a commitment.

"Termination" means the date on which the final suspension notice is issued by the billing system, not the date of the first unpaid invoice and not the date payment is later received. The requester, Ivo Marchetti, asked this morning (Monday 14 September 2026) for ticket HD-60392 to be reopened. The Ticket Lifecycle Standard, version 4, sets the rules. The base rule in 5.1 is that a resolved ticket closes automatically after five business days without a response from the requester, and a closed ticket may be reopened by the requester within ten business days of the closure date. After that, a new ticket must be raised.

Clause 5.2 provides an exception for recurrence: a closed ticket may be reopened at any time, without regard to the ten-day window, where the same fault recurs. The clause defines "same fault" as the same error code or the same knowledge-base article reference as recorded on the original ticket.

Clause 5.4 concerns priority escalation, a different process: a requester who believes an open ticket is under-prioritised may ask for escalation, which is reviewed by the queue lead within one business day. Escalation does not reopen closed tickets and has its own form.

Clause 2, definitions, states that "business days" are Monday to Friday excluding the company holidays listed in the annual calendar. The 2026 calendar lists Monday 7 September 2026 as a company holiday. The clause also provides that where an amendment changes a number in clause 5, the amended number applies to closures occurring on or after the amendment's effective date.

Amendment TLS-4.1, effective 1 August 2026, reduces the reopen window in clause 5.1 from ten business days to seven business days. The amendment states that clause 5.2 is unchanged.

The queue lead counts the business days between the closure and the request and asks whether the reopen is permitted.

question.instructions: Under the Ticket Lifecycle Standard as amended, may ticket HD-60392 be reopened?

criteria.true: The reopen falls within the applicable window or an exception permits it.
criteria.false: The reopen falls outside the applicable window and no exception applies.

provenance.rationale: The closure was 1 September, after the amendment, so the window is seven business days. Excluding the weekend days and the 7 September holiday, the business days after closure are 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11 September (seven) and 14 September is the eighth, outside the window. The recurrence exception needs the same error code; VPN-118 and VPN-207 differ, so 5.2 does not apply.

Paragraph 3 concerns a neighbouring case type: defects that will not be fixed because the behaviour is intended or the affected version is unsupported are closed as "won't fix" rather than as duplicates, and paragraph 1 and 2 do not apply to them.
